title: Sherlock and Cost
directAnswer: Given array A, build B with 1 ≤ B[i] ≤ A[i] maximizing Σ|B[i] − B[i−1]|. The key observation: to maximize a sum of absolute differences, every B[i] should sit at one of its two extremes — either 1 or A[i] — never in between. So track two running DP values: high[i] = best total when B[i] = A[i], and low[i] = best total when B[i] = 1. Transition each from the previous high/low by adding the absolute gap. Answer = max(high[n−1], low[n−1]). O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Two-state (high/low) DP — each element pinned to an extreme
remember.formula:
high = low = 0   # high: B[i]=A[i], low: B[i]=1
for i in 1..n-1:
    nh = max(high + |A[i] - A[i-1]|, low + |A[i] - 1|)
    nl = max(high + |1 - A[i-1]|,   low + |1 - 1|)
    high, low = nh, nl
answer = max(high, low)
rules: To **maximize** a sum of absolute differences, each B[i] is best at an **endpoint** of its range: 1 or A[i]. Interior values can never beat both extremes simultaneously.
Keep exactly **two** states per index — `high` (chose A[i]) and `low` (chose 1) — because the next element's gain depends only on the previous element's chosen value.
Each transition tries **both** previous choices and keeps the max: the previous element could have been high or low.
Initialise `high = low = 0` at index 0 — there's no earlier element, so the first |difference| term is 0 either way.
When `A[i] == 1`, high and low collapse to the same value (the only choice is 1); the recurrence handles this automatically.
whenToUse: Maximize/minimize a sum of |adjacent differences| with per-element value ranges
Each position has a small fixed set of optimal candidate values (here, two extremes)
A linear chain where the next term's contribution depends only on the previous choice
State-machine DP with a constant number of states per index
antiSignals: Minimizing the sum of differences → the optimum is the opposite (cluster values), different reasoning
Differences are squared or weighted nonlinearly → endpoints may not be optimal; reconsider
Values are continuous with no integer constraint → still endpoints, but framing differs
Dependencies reach back more than one element → more states or a different model
remember.takeaway: When you're maximizing a sum of absolute differences and each term is bounded, the extremes win — so the continuous range [1, A[i]] collapses to just {1, A[i]}. That reduction turns an infinite choice space into a clean two-state DP solvable in O(1) space.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you prove that B[i] only ever needs to be 1 or A[i] (the extremes), then model the two choices as a two-state DP carrying high/low forward.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Trying intermediate values of B[i], or carrying only one state (forgetting the previous element could have been at the other extreme), which loses optimal transitions.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Justify the extremes-only claim via convexity of |x|, then collapse the O(n) two-state DP to two scalars and note A[i]=1 as the degenerate case.

problemStatement:
You are given an array `A` of `n` integers. Construct an array `B` of the same length where each element satisfies `1 ≤ B[i] ≤ A[i]`.

Define the **cost** as:

`S = Σ |B[i] − B[i−1]|` for `i` from 1 to n−1.

Return the **maximum** possible value of `S` over all valid arrays `B`.
constraints: Each B[i] is an integer with 1 ≤ B[i] ≤ A[i]
Cost is the sum of absolute differences of consecutive B values
understanding: You're free to pick each B[i] anywhere from 1 up to A[i], and you want consecutive picks to be as far apart as possible. Intuitively, to make neighbours far apart you push each one to an extreme — the smallest (1) or the largest (A[i]) it's allowed to be. The only decision left at each position is which extreme, and that decision interacts only with the immediately previous one.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Why is B[i] always best at 1 or A[i], never in between?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The cost is a sum of absolute-value terms, and |x| is convex. For a fixed neighbour, moving B[i] toward an endpoint never decreases the contribution — at least one endpoint is at least as good as any interior point. With two neighbours, the optimum is still attained at an endpoint. So we only ever consider 1 and A[i].

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do we need to reconstruct B, or just the maximum cost?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just the maximum cost here. The two-state DP yields the value; recovering B would need to remember the choices.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What happens when A[i] = 1?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Then B[i] must be 1 — high and low coincide. The recurrence still works because choosing A[i]=1 and choosing 1 are the same.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could the answer be 0?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — if n = 1 there are no differences, or if every A[i] = 1 the only B is all-ones with cost 0.

examples.explanation: Take B = [10, 1, 10, 1, 10]: differences 9+9+9+9 = 36. The forced 1s create large swings against the 10s.
First three are forced to 1; last can be up to 5. B = [1,1,1,5] gives 0+0+4 = 4.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Recurse over the Two Extremes
approaches.whenToMention: State it to justify the extremes-only reduction and expose the overlapping subproblems.
hints: First argue you only ever set B[i] to 1 or A[i]. Then the search is: for each index, pick one of two values.
Recurse carrying the value chosen for the previous element. At index i, try B[i]=1 and B[i]=A[i], add |B[i] − prev|, and recurse.
That's 2 branches per index → 2ⁿ paths, but the state is just (index, previous choice ∈ {1, A[i-1]}) — only 2n distinct states.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Two branches at each of n indices form a binary tree of 2ⁿ leaves; recursion depth O(n).
approaches.explanation:
Lean on the extremes-only insight: every `B[i]` is either `1` or `A[i]`. The brute force enumerates all `2ⁿ` such assignments by recursion.

**The recursion.** Define `f(i, prev)` = the best cost achievable from index `i` onward, given the previous element was set to `prev`. At index `i` we try both choices `v ∈ {1, A[i]}`, pay `|v − prev|`, and recurse: `f(i, prev) = max over v of ( |v − prev| + f(i+1, v) )`. The base case `f(n, prev) = 0`.

**Why endpoints only.** For a fixed `prev`, the contribution `|v − prev|` is maximized at one of the endpoints of `[1, A[i]]`. The next term also depends on `v`, but it too is a sum of absolute values, which is convex in `v` — and a convex function on an interval attains its maximum at an endpoint. By induction the whole tail is convex in `v`, so testing `1` and `A[i]` suffices. This is the crucial argument that shrinks an infinite range to two values.

**Why we don't ship it.** Branching two ways per index gives `2ⁿ` paths — hopeless at `n = 10⁵`. But `f(i, prev)` only ever sees `prev ∈ {1, A[i-1]}`, so there are just `2n` distinct subproblems, each recomputed exponentially often. Cache them (or carry two rolling values) and the cost drops to `O(n)`.
approaches.insight: The infinite range [1, A[i]] collapses to two candidates because the cost is convex in each B[i], and convex functions peak at endpoints. That single observation is what makes the problem a finite two-state DP instead of an optimization over reals.

dryRun.intro: f(i, prev): best tail cost. B[i] ∈ {1, A[i]}. Showing the winning path.

pitfalls: Trying interior values of B[i] — unnecessary and exponentially slower.
Forgetting to seed both choices for B[0].
Running unmemoized at large n — 2ⁿ never returns.

approaches.name: Two-State Rolling DP (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'carry high and low forward, each transitioned from both previous states'.
hints: Define high = best total when the current B is A[i], low = best total when the current B is 1.
To extend to index i, the previous element could have been high (value A[i-1]) or low (value 1). Try both and keep the max.
new_high = max(high + |A[i]-A[i-1]|, low + |A[i]-1|); new_low = max(high + |1-A[i-1]|, low + 0). Answer = max(high, low).
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass over n elements, O(1) work per step (two max computations) → O(n) time. Only two scalars retained → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Convert the memoized recursion into a forward sweep with two rolling values.

**State.** After processing index `i`, let `high` = the maximum cost of a valid prefix ending with `B[i] = A[i]`, and `low` = the maximum cost ending with `B[i] = 1`. These two numbers summarise everything the future needs to know about the past, because the next difference depends only on the current chosen value.

**Transition.** Moving to index `i`, the previous element was either at its high (`A[i-1]`) or low (`1`):
- New high (choose `B[i] = A[i]`): `max(high + |A[i] − A[i-1]|, low + |A[i] − 1|)`.
- New low (choose `B[i] = 1`): `max(high + |1 − A[i-1]|, low + |1 − 1|)` = `max(high + |1 − A[i-1]|, low)`.

Each new state takes the better of coming from the previous high or previous low — that's why we keep both, not just the running best.

**Initialisation.** At index 0 there is no previous element, so both `high` and `low` start at `0`; the first transition adds the first real difference.

**Answer.** After the loop, the optimal cost is `max(high, low)` — the last element may end at either extreme.

**Why O(1) space.** The recurrence reaches back exactly one index, so two scalars replace any array. No recursion means no stack-depth risk at `n = 10⁵`. Use a `long` accumulator: with `A[i]` up to `10⁹` and `n` up to `10⁵`, the sum can exceed 32-bit range.
approaches.insight: The reason two states beat one running maximum: the best continuation from index i depends on *which* extreme the previous element took, not just on the previous best cost. Carrying high and low separately preserves exactly that dependency — a hallmark of state-machine DP.

dryRun.intro: high = end at A[i]; low = end at 1. Start high=low=0.

java.explanation: Zero or one element → no differences → cost 0.

java.explanation: Choose B[i]=A[i]; previous was high (A[i-1]) or low (1) — take the better.

java.explanation: Choose B[i]=1; from previous high add |1−A[i-1]|, from previous low add 0.
Last element may end at either extreme — take the larger.

Best way to land on 1; low→low adds nothing (|1-1|=0).
Optimal cost over both final choices.

pitfalls: Carrying only one running max instead of separate high/low — loses transitions from the other extreme.
Using int accumulators — overflow when A[i]·n exceeds 2³¹; use long.
Forgetting the n ≤ 1 guard, which would index A[i-1] out of range.

commonMistakes: Considering interior values of B[i] instead of just the extremes 1 and A[i].
Tracking a single best cost rather than two states (high and low).
Integer overflow from summing large differences without a 64-bit accumulator.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Trying interior values of B[i]
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The cost is convex in each B[i], so the maximum is always at an endpoint. Searching interior values is both unnecessary and prevents an O(n) solution.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for v in range(1, A[i] + 1):   # entire range
    best = max(best, abs(v - prev) + ...)
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
for v in (1, A[i]):            # only the two extremes
    best = max(best, abs(v - prev) + ...)

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Collapsing to one state
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The next difference depends on which extreme the previous element took. Keeping a single 'best so far' discards the value needed to compute the next gap.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
long best = ...;
best = Math.max(best + |A[i]-A[i-1]|, ...);  // ambiguous: which prev value?
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
long nh = Math.max(high + |A[i]-A[i-1]|, low + |A[i]-1|);
long nl = Math.max(high + |1-A[i-1]|, low);

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Integer overflow
commonMistakesDetailed.why: With A[i] up to 10⁹ and n up to 10⁵, the total cost can reach ~10¹⁴ — far beyond 32-bit int.
